✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

Scary Movie (2026) is not a woke trap. The film contains woke-coded elements (nonbinary character, trans character, rebootquel meta-commentary) but every one of these elements is present as an object of satire rather than ideological endorsement. The nonbinary character is literally murdered for having 'liberal perspectives,' the trans character is a throwaway joke, and the rebootquel concept is actively subverted when the legacy characters kill the would-be replacements. The film's actual thesis, delivered in its final minutes, is that the original creators will not be replaced. Nothing is concealed; the film is exactly what it appears to be: a Wayans family parody that mocks everyone, including woke culture.

Our Verdict on Scary Movie (2026)

Scary Movie (2026) is not a good movie in any conventional sense. It is a loud, crude, aggressively stupid 96-minute assault on taste, logic, and the human attention span. It is also the most ideologically interesting comedy released by a major studio this year, and accidentally the most traditionally-grounded Scary Movie since the original.

The film's meta-narrative is more compelling than its actual narrative. After a 25-year absence, the Wayans family returned to the franchise they created, having walked away after Scary Movie 2 when Dimension Films wanted to take the series in directions they opposed. Scary Movies 3, 4, and 5 were made without them, each one further from the original's spirit. This film is their answer: a 'spiritual sequel' that ignores the intervening films and positions itself as the true heir to the first two. The plot concerns a Ghostface-style killer murdering the children and associates of the original characters, with the young new cast seemingly being positioned as the franchise's future. The young characters explicitly say they want to 'take over the Scary Movie franchise from the legacy characters.' The film's final scene has Cindy, Brenda, Shorty, and Ray tying up the would-be replacements and leaving them to burn to death in a house, declaring that no one will take the franchise from them.

Read that again. The Wayans family made a $30 million studio comedy whose actual thesis is: the new generation doesn't get to steal what we built. The creators own the creation. The originals survive. That is not a progressive message. That is an argument for creative patrimony delivered at the end of a movie where someone gets killed by a ghost in a K-Pop animated sequence.

Along the way, the film takes swipes at virtually every woke piety available to a 2026 Hollywood production. The nonbinary character (Dei, Brenda's child) is stabbed to death on a subway by Ghostface and fellow passengers who are 'fed up with their liberal perspectives.' The transgender character (Jess, the sheriff's son) is murdered offscreen. Gail Hailstorm undergoes a grotesque cosmetic procedure to 'look young again' that ends with her alternate self being injected with toxic goo and killed, a sequence that reads as a direct mockery of Hollywood's obsession with youth and bodily reinvention. The young heroes who believe the franchise belongs to them by generational right are the villains, and they are punished for their presumption with death by immolation.

Is any of this high-minded? No. It's a Scary Movie. The jokes about bodily functions, sex, and celebrity cameos (Kai Cenat is murdered on a livestream) outnumber any coherent ideological statements about ten to one. But the film's id, its unconscious set of assumptions about what is worth mocking and what is worth valuing, is unmistakably traditional. The legacy characters are the heroes. The family that built something together is the unit worth preserving. The kids who think they deserve a turn because they exist are the punchline. Ray may renounce homosexuality for a joke, but the joke lands because the film takes for granted that a man and woman raising children together is the natural order being restored, not transgressed.

The film is too stupid to be called a conservative polemic, and too self-aware in its stupidity to be dismissed as accidental. What it is, is a Wayans family comedy made by people who have been in Hollywood long enough to see every trend come and go, and who have decided not to take any of them seriously. That instinct, to mock everything and respect nothing except the family that made you, turns out to produce a more traditionally-grounded film than any number of self-consciously 'anti-woke' productions. The Scary Movie franchise was never ideological. It was always just funny. In 2026, just being funny without genuflecting to the reigning orthodoxies is itself a kind of rebellion.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Michael Tiddes

MODERATE. Tiddes is a longtime Wayans collaborator (A Haunted House, Sextuplets) who follows the Wayans creative lead. His work reflects the family's ethos of equal-opportunity comedy rather than personal ideological conviction.

Michael Tiddes has been the Wayans family's go-to director since A Haunted House (2013). He understands their comic rhythm and trusts their instincts. His direction on Scary Movie 2026 is workmanlike rather than visionary, which serves the material: the jokes are the star, and Tiddes stays out of their way.

Writer: Marlon Wayans, Shawn Wayans, Keenen Ivory Wayans, Craig Wayans, Rick Alvarez

The Wayans writing team returns to the franchise after a 25-year absence. Their departure after Scary Movie 2 (2001) was due to creative conflicts with Dimension Films over the direction of the series. Scary Movie 3-5 were made without them. Their return represents a creative reclamation: the original architects taking back the house. The writing reflects the original Scary Movie spirit of fearless, boundary-pushing parody that targets everyone equally. The script takes particular pleasure in skewering Hollywood's reboot obsession, identity-driven casting conventions, and the very concept of the 'requel' that brings back legacy characters to pass the torch. The torch is not passed. It is set on fire.

Content Breakdown

Adult Viewer Insight

Scary Movie (2026) grossed $215.4 million against a $30 million budget, making it one of the most profitable films of 2026. The audience showed up for nostalgia and raunchy comedy, not ideological analysis, and that is precisely the point. The film's commercial success suggests there is a large appetite for comedy that refuses to take itself seriously, that mocks the pieties of the moment, and that trusts its audience to distinguish between a joke at someone's expense and an endorsement of cruelty. The film is not a political document. It is a reminder that sometimes the most subversive thing you can do in 2026 is refuse to be ideologically legible.

Parental Guidance

Rated R for strong crude sexual content, pervasive language, drug use, comic violence, and some graphic nudity. Not appropriate for children or young teenagers. The Scary Movie franchise has always been deliberately offensive across all categories, and this installment is no different. Adults who remember the original films will know what they're getting into. New viewers should understand that no identity, ideology, or institution is spared.
